misconceptions.description: Assumes every cell in a plant contains chloroplasts.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Only cells that receive light have chloroplasts. Root cells have none, which is why roots are not green; the plant makes sugar in the leaves and transports it down.

misconceptions.description: Reads a food chain arrow as pointing from the eater to what it eats.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The arrow shows which way the energy moves, so it points from the food to the feeder. In grass to rabbit to fox, the rabbit eats the grass and the fox eats the rabbit.

misconceptions.description: Gives a gamete the same chromosome number as a body cell.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: If gametes carried the full number, fertilisation would double it every generation. Gametes carry half, so that sperm and egg together restore the normal count.

misconceptions.description: Orders a gene as larger than a chromosome.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule carrying many genes, so the chromosome is much larger. The nesting runs: DNA makes up genes, and genes sit along chromosomes.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: A chromosome is part of a gene

misconceptions.description: Says meiosis produces two daughter cells, copying the mitosis outcome.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Meiosis involves two rounds of division, so one cell becomes four. Mitosis has a single division and gives two. Counting the divisions is the reliable way to remember which is which.

misconceptions.description: Treats movement as sufficient evidence that something is alive.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Movement is only one of seven life processes, and non-living things move too - rivers, fires and machines all do. Something is alive only if it does all seven, including respiration and reproduction.

misconceptions.description: Calls a structure made of several tissue types a tissue.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A tissue is one kind of cell working together. As soon as several different tissues combine for a shared function, it is an organ. The heart contains muscle, nerve and blood tissue, so it is an organ.

misconceptions.description: Believes plants respire only in darkness, when photosynthesis stops.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Plants respire all the time, day and night, because every living cell needs energy continuously. In daylight photosynthesis runs faster than respiration, so the net exchange looks reversed - but respiration never stopped.

misconceptions.description: Reads a Punnett ratio as a guarantee about a small number of offspring.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A Punnett square gives the probability for each offspring independently. Over many offspring the proportions approach the ratio, but any particular set of four can come out in any combination, just as four coin tosses need not be two heads and two tails.

misconceptions.description: Uses respiration and breathing interchangeably.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food inside cells, and it happens in every living cell - including in organisms with no lungs at all.

misconceptions.description: Applies the energy loss once when the food chain requires it twice.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Count the arrows. Reaching a secondary consumer means two transfers from the producer, so the ten per cent applies twice - a hundredth overall, not a tenth.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the number after a closing bracket, so grouped atoms are counted only once.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A number after a closing bracket multiplies everything inside it, just as in algebra. In Ca(OH)2 the 2 applies to both the O and the H, giving two of each rather than one.

misconceptions.description: Balances an equation by altering a subscript rather than a coefficient.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A subscript is part of the substance's identity - changing O2 to O3 turns oxygen into ozone. Only the coefficient in front may be changed, because that just counts how many units react.

misconceptions.description: Concludes mass was destroyed when a gaseous product escapes the container.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The mass left as a gas; it was not destroyed. Repeat the reaction in a sealed container and the balance reading does not change at all, which is the standard demonstration of conservation of mass.

misconceptions.description: Thinks elements in the same group have the same number of protons.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The proton count is what makes elements different, so no two elements share it. A group shares the number of OUTER electrons, which is what governs reactions.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: They have the same number of protons

misconceptions.description: Reads the mass number as the number of neutrons, without subtracting the protons.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, because both sit in the nucleus and both have about the same mass. Subtract the atomic number to leave the neutrons alone.

misconceptions.description: Calls any substance containing more than one element a compound, whether or not it is bonded.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A compound needs a chemical bond and a fixed ratio, and it has properties of its own. If the substances are merely together, keep their own properties, and can be separated physically, it is a mixture.

misconceptions.description: Believes the particles themselves expand, shrink or change when a substance changes state.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A change of state rearranges particles; it does not alter them. The water particles in ice, liquid water and steam are identical - what differs is how much energy they have and how tightly they are held together.

misconceptions.description: Reads a higher pH as more acidic, inverting the scale.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The pH scale runs the other way: 0 is strongly acidic, 7 is neutral, and 14 is strongly alkaline. A lower number means more acidic, so pH 2 is far more acidic than pH 6.

misconceptions.description: Adds one of each atomic mass, ignoring the subscripts, when totalling a formula mass.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Each atom contributes its own mass, so a subscript multiplies that element's contribution. CO2 has two oxygens, so oxygen contributes 2 x 16 = 32, not 16.

misconceptions.description: Treats taking away or sharing as addition, because the situation involves two numbers.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Addition joins groups to make a larger total. If the situation removes, compares, or shares out, it is not addition. Ask whether the amount ends up bigger or smaller.

misconceptions.description: Operates on one side of an equation only, breaking the balance.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other, or the two sides stop being equal.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: multiply only the left side by 2

misconceptions.description: Combines terms with different variable parts, treating 3x + 2y as 5xy or 5x.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Only like terms combine, meaning terms with exactly the same variable part. 3x and 2y count different things and have to stay separate.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies the bracket's first term only, so 2(x + 3) becomes 2x + 3.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The multiplier applies to every term inside the bracket. 2(x + 3) is 2x + 6. Draw an arrow from the multiplier to each term so none is missed.

misconceptions.description: Adds successive percentage changes instead of applying them one after another.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Each change applies to the amount at the time, so percentages do not simply add. Apply the first change, then apply the second to the result.

misconceptions.description: Lines up decimals by their right-hand ends when adding or subtracting.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Line up the decimal points so that tenths sit under tenths and units under units. Pad with zeros if the numbers have different lengths.

misconceptions.description: Reports the new amount, or the whole, where the question asks for the size of the change.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Percentage change compares the change with the starting amount, not with the finishing amount. Work out the difference first, then divide by the original value.

misconceptions.description: Turns a fraction into a decimal by copying its digits, so 1/4 becomes 0.4.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A fraction is a division. Work out 1 divided by 4, which is 0.25. Copying the digits ignores what the denominator does.

misconceptions.description: Does not count the total decimal places when multiplying decimals.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Multiply as if the numbers were whole, then give the answer as many decimal places as the two factors had together. 0.2 x 0.3 has two decimal places in total, so the answer is 0.06.

misconceptions.description: Divides the whole by the part when finding what percentage one number is of another.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The part goes on top. Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. Putting them the other way round gives a figure over 100% whenever the part is smaller.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: divide the whole by the part, then multiply by 100

misconceptions.description: Assumes the decimal with more digits is larger, so 0.45 beats 0.5.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Compare place by place from the left, not by length. 0.5 has 5 tenths and 0.45 has only 4 tenths, so 0.5 is larger even though it is shorter.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies by the percentage when the whole is the unknown.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: If you know the part and the percentage, divide the part by the percentage written as a decimal. Multiplying gives a whole smaller than the part, which cannot be right.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: multiply the part by the percent

misconceptions.description: Multiplies by the percent number itself rather than by its decimal form.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Convert the percentage first. To find 30% of an amount, multiply by 0.3, not by 30, or you get an answer a hundred times too big.

misconceptions.description: Converts a percentage to a decimal by moving the point one place instead of two.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Percent means out of one hundred, so dividing by 100 moves the point two places. 7% is 0.07, not 0.7.

misconceptions.description: Ignores a zero placeholder after the decimal point, reading 0.06 as 0.6.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Each place after the point is ten times smaller than the one before. The zero in 0.06 holds the tenths place, so the 6 sits in hundredths and the number is much smaller than 0.6.

misconceptions.description: Rounds using the last digit of the number rather than the digit after the rounding place.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Look only at the digit immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to. Digits further along do not vote.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: the last digit of the number

misconceptions.description: Adds numerators and denominators separately, so 1/5 + 2/5 becomes 3/10.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The denominator names the size of the pieces, and adding does not change that size. With fifths, 1 fifth plus 2 fifths is 3 fifths: add the numerators and keep the denominator.

misconceptions.description: Adds the same number to numerator and denominator and expects an equivalent fraction.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Equivalent fractions come from multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number, which keeps the ratio. Adding changes the ratio: 1/2 and 2/3 are not equal.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: it does make an equivalent fraction

misconceptions.description: Judges a fraction larger because its denominator is larger.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more, and therefore smaller, pieces. One third is smaller than one half, because thirds are smaller pieces than halves.

misconceptions.description: Scales the denominator to a common one but leaves the numerator unchanged.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Whatever you multiply the denominator by, you must multiply the numerator by too, or you have changed the value. To turn 1/2 into eighths, multiply both parts by 4 to get 4/8.

misconceptions.description: Names a fraction from a shape split into unequal parts, counting pieces rather than equal shares.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A fraction names equal parts of a whole. If the pieces are different sizes, one of them is not a quarter just because there are four. Check that every part is the same size first.

misconceptions.description: Reads an ordered pair as (y, x), moving up before across.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The first number is always the horizontal move and the second the vertical one. For (3, 5) go 3 right and then 5 up.

misconceptions.description: Believes absolute value can come out negative.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Absolute value is a distance from zero, and a distance is never negative. Both -7 and 7 are 7 away from zero, so both have absolute value 7.

misconceptions.description: Compares negative numbers by their digits, so -8 is judged larger than -2.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: On a number line, further left is smaller. Negative numbers with bigger digits are further left, so -8 is less than -2. Picture the line before you compare.

misconceptions.description: Assumes dividing a negative by a negative gives a negative.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Division follows the same sign rule as multiplication. Two like signs give a positive result, so -12 divided by -3 is 4.

misconceptions.description: Assumes multiplying two negatives keeps the answer negative.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Multiplying by a negative reverses direction. Reversing twice returns to the original direction, so a negative times a negative is positive: -3 x -4 = 12.

misconceptions.description: Adds the side lengths where area calls for multiplying them.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Area counts the squares that cover a shape, which is length multiplied by width. Adding the sides gives the distance round the edge, which is perimeter.

misconceptions.description: Converts in the wrong direction, so the number moves the opposite way to the unit.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Going to a smaller unit needs more of them, so multiply; going to a larger unit needs fewer, so divide. Check the answer against that expectation before writing it down.

misconceptions.description: Adds the number of rows and columns in an array instead of multiplying them.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An array has rows of equal size, so the total is rows multiplied by the number in each row. A 3 by 4 array has 3 groups of 4, which is 12, not 3 + 4.

misconceptions.description: Decides even or odd from the leading digit instead of the last digit.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Only the ones digit decides. A number is even when it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, whatever the other digits are. 34 is even because it ends in 4.

misconceptions.description: Counts 1 as prime, because it appears to have no factors other than itself.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A prime has exactly two different factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. The smallest prime is 2.

misconceptions.description: Evaluates strictly left to right, ignoring that multiplication and division bind before addition and subtraction.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Work through brackets first, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. In 2 + 3 x 4 the multiplication happens first, giving 14, not 20.

misconceptions.description: Reads a digit at its face value instead of its place value, so the 5 in 57 is treated as 5 rather than 50.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A digit's value depends on the column it sits in. In 57 the 5 is in the tens column, so it is worth 5 tens, or 50. Say the column name aloud as you read each digit.

misconceptions.description: Applies the outer function first, so f(g(x)) is evaluated as g(f(x)).
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The function written closest to the input acts first. In f(g(3)) the g touches the 3, so compute g(3) and feed that into f. Working left to right computes the other composition.

misconceptions.description: Adds the same interest each period instead of applying the rate to the new balance.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Each year's growth applies to the balance at the time, which already includes earlier growth. Two years at 5 percent is not 10 percent of the original - it is 1.05 times 1.05, so a little more.

misconceptions.description: Undoes a cube by dividing by 3 instead of taking a cube root.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Cubing multiplies a number by itself three times, so undoing it needs a cube root, not a division. 27 divided by 3 is 9, but 9 cubed is 729, not 27.

misconceptions.description: Reports the degree of the largest factor instead of adding the degrees of a product.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Multiplying powers adds their exponents, so the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees. (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2) has degree 2 + 3 = 5, not 3.

misconceptions.description: Calls a doubling pattern arithmetic because the early differences look like a pattern of their own.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Arithmetic needs the same amount added every time. In 2, 4, 8, 16 the differences are 2, 4, 8 - growing, not constant - while the ratios are all 2, which makes it geometric.

misconceptions.description: Treats every zero of the denominator as a vertical asymptote, even when the factor cancels.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Check whether the factor also divides the numerator. If it cancels, the graph has a single missing point - a hole - because the function agrees with a simpler expression everywhere else.

misconceptions.description: Reads a constant difference where the pattern actually has a constant ratio.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Check whether consecutive terms differ by the same amount or are multiplied by the same amount. In 2, 6, 18, 54 the differences are 4, 12, 36 - not constant - while the ratios are all 3.

misconceptions.description: Reads f^-1 as one divided by f, turning an inverse into a reciprocal.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The -1 in f^-1 means 'the function that undoes f', not a power. f^-1(11) asks which input gives 11. If you want a reciprocal, that is written 1/f(x).

misconceptions.description: Uses the value of the last term as the number of terms in a series formula.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The formula needs how many terms there are, not how big the last one is. From 5 to 41 in steps of 4 there are 10 terms, so use 10.

misconceptions.description: Applies the product rule to a sum, so log(a + b) becomes log(a) + log(b).
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The product rule needs a product. log(a) + log(b) equals log(ab), not log(a + b). Test it with a = b = 10 in base 10: log(20) is about 1.301, but log(10) + log(10) = 2.

misconceptions.description: Divides the number by the base instead of finding the exponent.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A logarithm asks for an exponent, not a quotient. log base 2 of 8 asks what power of 2 gives 8, which is 3 because 2^3 = 8. Dividing gives 4, and 2^4 is 16.

misconceptions.description: Folds the coefficient into the base, treating a times b^x as (ab)^x.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Only the base carries the exponent. In 3 times 2^x you raise 2 to the power first and then multiply by 3. Turning it into 6^x multiplies the 3 in as many times as the exponent says.

misconceptions.description: Stops at the value of the whole exponent instead of solving for the variable inside it.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Matching the bases tells you what the exponent equals, not what x equals. In 3^(x+1) = 81 you get x + 1 = 4, so there is still one step left: x = 3.

misconceptions.description: Gives only the positive solution of x^2 = k, missing the negative one.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A square has two square roots. x^2 = 9 is true for x = 3 and for x = -3, because a negative times a negative is positive. Always check both signs.

misconceptions.description: Takes n steps to reach the nth term, so every answer overshoots by one step.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The first term is already there before any step is taken, so the nth term is only n - 1 steps along. For 4, 7, 10 the 10th term needs 9 threes added, not 10.

misconceptions.description: Reads the zero of (x - a) as -a, copying the sign in the bracket instead of solving.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Solve the bracket rather than reading it. x - 2 = 0 gives x = +2, and x + 5 = 0 gives x = -5, so the signs flip.

misconceptions.description: Writes a ratio in the opposite order to the one the question names.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A ratio keeps the order of the things being compared. If it asks for red to blue, the red count comes first: 3 red and 2 blue is 3:2, not 2:3.

misconceptions.description: Rounds up regardless of the deciding digit, instead of comparing it with 5.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Rounding looks at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more you round up; if it is 4 or less you round down. 64 rounds to 60 because the 4 is less than 5.

misconceptions.description: Gives the reference-angle value without its sign, so ratios stay positive outside quadrant I.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Only quadrant I has all three ratios positive. Work out the size from the reference angle, then set the sign from the quadrant: sine is positive in quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, tangent in I and III.

misconceptions.description: Reports a negative amplitude when the coefficient is negative.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Amplitude measures a distance from the midline to a peak, so it is never negative. A negative coefficient reflects the graph; take the size of the coefficient for the amplitude.

misconceptions.description: Reports the whole distance from minimum to maximum as the amplitude, doubling the true value.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Amplitude is measured from the midline to a peak, which is half the distance from lowest to highest. For y = 3 sin x the graph runs from -3 to 3, a span of 6, but the amplitude is 3.

misconceptions.description: Gives a rounded decimal where an exact value was asked for.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An exact value keeps the square root or the pi in it. sqrt(3)/2 is exact; 0.866 is a rounding of it and is not equal to it. Write the surd or the multiple of pi instead.

misconceptions.description: Treats a radian measure as if it were a number of degrees, or reports degrees when radians were asked for.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A radian is much bigger than a degree: pi radians is 180 degrees, so one radian is about 57 degrees. Convert with the ratio 180 degrees = pi radians before answering.

misconceptions.description: Applies the trig function to the ratio instead of the inverse function, so a ratio comes back where an angle was wanted.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Sine turns an angle into a ratio; inverse sine turns a ratio into an angle. If you know the ratio and want the angle, use the inverse. Check your answer by feeding it forwards through sine again.

misconceptions.description: Takes the longest-looking or first-listed side as the hypotenuse rather than the one opposite the right angle.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest side. Find the right angle first, then look straight across from it.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: the side next to the right angle

misconceptions.description: Multiplies by the ratio when the unknown is the hypotenuse, giving a hypotenuse shorter than a leg.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. If the unknown is the hypotenuse, it sits underneath in the ratio, so you divide by the sine or cosine rather than multiplying. A hypotenuse shorter than one of the legs is impossible.

misconceptions.description: Leaves the period at 360 degrees when a coefficient on x has compressed the graph.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A coefficient on x changes how fast the input runs, so it changes the period. Divide 360 degrees by that coefficient: y = sin 2x completes a cycle in 180 degrees.

misconceptions.description: Reads the unit-circle point as (sine, cosine), swapping the two coordinates.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The horizontal coordinate is written first and it is the cosine; the vertical coordinate is the sine. The point at angle A is (cos A, sin A).

misconceptions.description: Uses sine where the adjacent side is involved, so cosine problems get the opposite side.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Sine pairs the opposite side with the hypotenuse; cosine pairs the adjacent side with the hypotenuse. Check which of the two non-hypotenuse sides the question names before picking the ratio.

misconceptions.description: Swaps the opposite and adjacent sides, so sine and tangent use the wrong side.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Opposite and adjacent are named relative to the angle you are working with. The opposite side does not touch the angle; the adjacent side does, and is not the hypotenuse. Label the triangle from the angle before choosing a ratio.

misconceptions.description: Reports tan 90 as 0 or 1 rather than recognising that it has no value.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Tangent is opposite over adjacent, and at 90 degrees the adjacent side is zero. Dividing by zero gives no answer at all, so tan 90 is undefined rather than any particular number.

misconceptions.description: Treats sine as if it distributed over multiplication, so sin 2A becomes 2 sin A.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Sine is a function, not a multiplier, so it cannot be pulled apart that way. Test it: sin 60 is about 0.866 but 2 sin 30 is 1. The correct expansion is sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A.

misconceptions.description: Believes acceleration requires a change in speed, so circular motion at constant speed looks unaccelerated.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity includes direction. Turning changes the direction, so it changes the velocity, so it is an acceleration even when the speedometer never moves.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: No, because its speed is constant

misconceptions.description: Adds frequency and wavelength instead of multiplying them.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Check the units. Waves per second multiplied by metres per wave gives metres per second, which is a speed. Adding hertz to metres gives nothing meaningful.

misconceptions.description: Adds forces that act in opposite directions instead of subtracting.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Direction matters when combining forces. Forces the same way add; forces in opposite directions partly cancel, so subtract the smaller from the larger and keep the direction of the larger.

misconceptions.description: Takes the mean of two speeds instead of dividing total distance by total time.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Average speed is always total distance divided by total time. Averaging the speeds treats both legs as lasting equally long, which is only true when they do. Here the slow leg took four times as long, so it should count four times as much.

misconceptions.description: Divides time by distance instead of distance by time when finding a speed.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The unit tells you the order. Metres per second means metres divided by seconds, so distance goes on top. Dividing the other way gives seconds per metre, which answers a different question.

misconceptions.description: Reports a slowing object's acceleration as positive, dropping the sign.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Subtract in the order final minus starting. If the object slowed, that difference is negative and the acceleration is negative too. The sign is what tells you it is slowing rather than speeding up.

misconceptions.description: Reports the full round-trip distance as the distance to the reflecting surface.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An echo travels out and back, so the sound covers twice the distance to the surface. Halve the total to get the one-way distance.

misconceptions.description: Believes friction destroys energy rather than transferring it.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Energy is never destroyed. Friction transfers it to the surroundings as heat, spreading it out so thinly that it can no longer do useful work - which feels like loss but is not.

misconceptions.description: Judges density by mass alone, ignoring volume.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Density is mass per unit volume, so a heavier object spread over a much larger volume can be less dense. Always divide before comparing.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: Object B, because it is heavier

misconceptions.description: Believes mass changes with location because weight does.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, and moving somewhere else does not add or remove matter, so mass never changes. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, so only weight changes when gravity does.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies distance by time when asked for speed.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Speed is a rate, so it is a division. Multiplying distance by time gives a quantity with no physical meaning here. Check your answer against the units: m/s needs metres divided by seconds.

misconceptions.description: Believes constant velocity requires a resultant force.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A resultant force changes motion; it is not needed to maintain it. At a steady speed the driving force is exactly cancelled by friction and drag, so the resultant is zero even though individual forces are large.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: There is a forward resultant force

misconceptions.description: Pairs the normal force with the object's weight, though both act on the same object.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A third law pair always acts on two different objects and is the same type of force. The table pushing the book pairs with the book pushing the table. The book's weight is the Earth pulling the book, and its partner is the book pulling the Earth.

misconceptions.description: Divides the final velocity by the time instead of the change in velocity.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Acceleration measures how much the velocity changed, so subtract the starting velocity first. Using the final velocity alone assumes the object started from rest, which is only sometimes true.

misconceptions.description: Uses velocity instead of velocity squared in the kinetic energy formula.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so KE = (1/2)mv^2. That is why doubling a car's speed quadruples its kinetic energy, and why stopping distances grow so sharply.

misconceptions.description: Treats doing something faster as doing more work.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Work is force times distance and says nothing about time. Doing the same job faster is more power, not more work.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: The faster one does more work

misconceptions.description: Assumes each gridline is one unit without reading the axis scale.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Check the scale before reading any value. If each square is 2 units, treating it as 1 halves every value you take off the graph.

misconceptions.description: Claims an experiment proves a hypothesis.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Data can support or fail to support a hypothesis, but a single experiment cannot prove it. Confidence grows as independent results agree.

misconceptions.description: Concludes from a scatter plot that one variable causes the other.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A trend in a scatter plot shows association. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together because both follow hot weather, not because one causes the other.

misconceptions.description: Deletes an outlier without investigating it.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An outlier may be a recording mistake or a real and interesting result. Investigate the cause and repeat the measurement; removing points silently hides evidence.

misconceptions.description: Reads a single dip or spike as a change in the overall trend.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A trend is the direction of the data as a whole. One point moving against it is usually normal variation; look at the shape across the whole range.

misconceptions.description: Joins the tops of bars with a line, implying values between separate categories.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Bar graphs compare separate categories, and there is nothing in between them to plot. Lines are for data that changes continuously, such as over time.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: the line is the wrong color

misconceptions.description: Accepts a data table whose columns carry no units.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A number without a unit is ambiguous: 5 could be seconds or minutes. Every measured column needs its unit in the heading.

misconceptions.description: Classifies a numeric label, such as a room number, as numerical data.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Numerical data measures a quantity you could sensibly average. A label that happens to be written as a number is categorical: averaging room numbers means nothing.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a number

misconceptions.description: Treats any straight-line graph as showing a proportional relationship.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A proportional relationship is a straight line through the origin, so that doubling one quantity doubles the other. A straight line with an intercept is linear but not proportional.

misconceptions.description: Expects averaging repeated trials to remove a systematic error.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Averaging cancels random scatter, but a systematic error pushes every reading the same way, so the average is off by the same amount. Find and fix the cause, for example by recalibrating.

misconceptions.description: Changes more than one variable at a time and still expects a clear conclusion.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: If two things change together you cannot tell which caused the effect. Change one variable and hold the rest constant.

misconceptions.description: Draws a conclusion from a treated group with nothing to compare it against.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Without an untreated control you cannot know what would have happened anyway. The control is what makes the comparison meaningful.

misconceptions.description: Concludes from a single trial.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: One trial can be unusual by chance. Repeating and comparing shows whether the result is reliable or a one-off.

misconceptions.description: Swaps the independent and dependent variables.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: The independent variable is the one you deliberately change; the dependent variable is what you measure in response. Ask which one you set before the experiment began.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: independent: leaf count; dependent: light level

misconceptions.description: Counts leading zeros as significant figures, so 0.0025 appears to have four.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Zeros before the first non-zero digit only locate the decimal point. In 0.0025 only the 2 and 5 are significant, so there are two significant figures.

misconceptions.description: Uses heat and temperature interchangeably.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Temperature measures how hot something is; heat is energy moving from hotter to cooler. A large warm object can hold more heat than a small hot one.

misconceptions.description: Treats mass and weight as the same, so mass is expected to change with gravity.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, so weight changes on the Moon while mass stays the same.

misconceptions.description: Reads a liquid volume at the top of the curved surface.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Read at the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with it. Reading from above or at the top of the curve gives a value that is consistently too high.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: at the top of the meniscus

misconceptions.description: Expects the number to grow when converting to a larger unit.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Larger units need fewer of them, so the number gets smaller. Converting 500 m to kilometres gives 0.5 km. Check that the size of the quantity has not changed.

misconceptions.description: Reads a correlation as proof that one variable causes the other.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: Two things can rise together because a third thing drives both, or by coincidence. Only a controlled experiment can support a claim about cause.

misconceptions.description: Judges a model wrong because it simplifies, expecting it to match reality exactly.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: A model deliberately leaves things out so that the important relationship stands out. It is judged by whether it is useful and predicts well, not by whether it is complete.

misconceptions.description: Accepts a restatement of the observation as an explanation, so a genuinely causal explanation looks weak by comparison.
misconceptions.corrective_explanation: An explanation must give a cause beyond the observation itself. Saying ice melted because it stopped being frozen only repeats what happened; naming heat conduction explains it.
misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: The ice melted faster on metal because metal conducts heat well.
